Shishir Kanti Talukder

Graduate Research Assistant at Texas Tech University

I'm a PhD student working on crop stress physiology, phenotyping and plant genomics. Take a look around to explore my recent work and research interests, and if you'd like to talk, you can reach me at the bottom of the page.

About

Hi, I'm Shishir, a PhD student in Plant & Soil Science at Texas Tech University. I work with Dr. Impa Somayanda, Dr. Krishna Jagadish and Dr. Dinesh Kumar Saini in the TeCSIS research program, studying how sorghum, cotton and chickpea respond to salinity, heat, drought and chilling stress. I'm especially interested in how phenotyping and genomics can work together to find the lines and genes that keep crops productive as water in West Texas becomes scarcer and saltier.

Outside of science, you'll usually find me behind a camera, at the zoo, exploring the many landscapes Texas has to offer, or starting a new hobby or side project. I also serve as President of the Association of Bangladeshi Students and Scholars at Texas Tech.

Projects

Current Projects

Salinity Tolerance in Sorghum and Cotton

Irrigation water in West Texas is getting saltier as the Ogallala Aquifer declines and growers turn to the deeper Dockum Aquifer, where water measures 7.5–9.3 dS/m, above sorghum's yield threshold. I am screening 300 sorghum accessions from the Sorghum Association Panel and 270 cotton accessions in a semi-hydroponic system, measuring biomass, Na⁺ and K⁺ concentrations and WinRHIZO root traits, then using GWAS and haplotype analysis to identify salt-tolerant lines and the genomic regions behind them.

  • Semi-hydroponics
  • WinRHIZO
  • Ion analysis
  • GWAS
  • Haplotypes

High-Biomass Chickpea for Forage

We planted 500 chickpea lines in the field and are phenotyping them across three seasons (summer, winter and spring) for biomass and related traits. The highest-biomass lines go for forage-quality analysis, and the three seasons of data feed GWAS and haplotype analysis. Lines that hold high biomass consistently across seasons will be selected for further breeding.

  • Field phenotyping
  • Biomass
  • Forage quality
  • GWAS
  • Haplotypes

Prussic Acid-Free Forage Sorghum

Prussic acid-free (PF) sorghum removes the risk of cyanide poisoning in livestock by disrupting dhurrin biosynthesis. With my colleagues, I am examining how this change reshapes sorghum metabolism and whether PF hybrids hold up under salinity, drought and combined stress, using field metabolomics, qRT-PCR, SPAD, biomass and forage-quality measurements in the greenhouse.

  • Metabolomics
  • qRT-PCR
  • Forage quality
  • Greenhouse

Reproductive-Stage Heat Tolerance

Extreme heat during flowering causes some of the largest yield losses in High Plains crops. Using custom field-based heat tents with continuous temperature monitoring, we are screening Texas cotton and sorghum to identify heat-tolerant donor lines for breeding programs.

  • Heat tents
  • Field phenotyping
  • Cotton
  • Sorghum
